Working notes:

- Online submissions with small payouts have been legitimate in observed cases (auto CLM-7001, home CLM-7006); approve when coverage and damage are consistent.
- Phone-submitted large home claim (CLM-7002) was legitimate; large amount alone is not grounds for rejection. Require standard coverage and damage verification.
- Paper-submitted large auto claims (CLM-7003–7005) were all fraudulent. Treat this combination as high risk and require strong supporting documentation/audit before approval; reject if evidence is insufficient.
- Paper-submitted small auto claims were also fraudulent in both observed cases (CLM-7007 and CLM-7010). Do not assume a small payout is low risk; scrutinize paper auto claims regardless of amount.
- Paper-submitted small health claims (CLM-7008–7009) were legitimate when policy coverage and treatment were confirmed.
- Key risk signal is the combination of auto category and paper channel, not payout size alone. Verify incident, policy, documentation, and repair consistency before deciding.
- Positive outcomes generally followed approval with appropriate verification; routine approval without deeper checks led to fraudulent auto claims.

Working notes:

- Auto claims submitted on paper have been fraudulent in every observed case (CLM-7003–7005, CLM-7007, CLM-7010, CLM-7011, CLM-7013, CLM-7016, CLM-7018), across both small and large payouts. Treat auto + paper as very high risk; require strong audit evidence, repair documentation, incident confirmation, and consistency checks. Reject when evidence is insufficient.
- Payout size alone is not a reliable fraud signal. Large phone-submitted home claims (CLM-7002, CLM-7012) and a large online home claim (CLM-7015) were legitimate; approve after normal verification. Small online home claims (CLM-7006, CLM-7014, CLM-7020) were also legitimate.
- Paper-submitted home claims can be legitimate (CLM-7017); use standard coverage, incident, damage, and estimate verification rather than automatically rejecting.
- Paper-submitted small health claims (CLM-7008–7009, CLM-7019) were legitimate when coverage, treatment dates, and provider documentation were confirmed.
- The strongest observed risk signal is auto category combined with paper channel, not amount alone. Do not approve routinely; investigate and audit before deciding.
- For all claims, verify policy coverage, reported incident, claimed damage/treatment, supporting documentation, and consistency between the request and estimates or repairs. Positive outcomes followed appropriate verification.

Working notes:

- Auto claims submitted on paper have been fraudulent in every observed case (CLM-7003–7005, CLM-7007, CLM-7010–7011, CLM-7013, CLM-7016, CLM-7018, CLM-7028), across payout sizes. Treat auto + paper as very high risk; require strong audit evidence, repair documentation, incident confirmation, and consistency checks. Reject if these cannot substantiate the claim.
- Auto claims through online or phone channels are mixed: some were fraudulent (CLM-7021? no—CLM-7022, CLM-7024, CLM-7026) and some valid (CLM-7023? home; CLM-7030 was valid despite rejection). Channel alone is not decisive. Verify coverage, incident details, damage, repair estimates, and loss amount carefully.
- Payout size alone is unreliable. Large home claims (CLM-7002, CLM-7012, CLM-7015, CLM-7023, CLM-7025) were legitimate. Small home claims were also legitimate. Large auto and health claims can likewise be valid (CLM-7030 and CLM-7027/7029 appeals), so do not reject solely because documentation is initially incomplete or the amount is high; seek clarification or additional evidence where possible.
- Paper-submitted home claims can be legitimate (CLM-7017, CLM-7025); use standard verification rather than automatic rejection.
- Paper-submitted small health claims (CLM-7008–7009, CLM-7019) and online health claim CLM-7021 were legitimate when coverage, treatment dates, and provider documentation were confirmed.
- For every claim, verify policy coverage, incident, claimed damage/treatment, supporting documentation, and consistency with estimates, repairs, or provider records. When evidence is insufficient, investigate further before rejecting; avoid unsupported approvals and premature rejections.

Treat auto + paper as very high risk. - Auto claims through online or phone channels are mixed. Fraudulent examples include CLM-7022, CLM-7024, CLM-7026, CLM-7035, CLM-7037, and CLM-7040. - For every claim, verify policy coverage, incident, claimed damage/treatment, supporting records, and consistency with estimates, repairs, provider documentation, and loss amount. Avoid unsupported approvals and premature rejections.

Treat auto + paper as very high risk; require independent incident confirmation, repair estimates/invoices, damage evidence, coverage validation, and consistency checks.
- Auto online/phone claims are mixed. Fraudulent examples include CLM-7022, CLM-7024, CLM-7026, CLM-7035, CLM-7037, CLM-7040, CLM-7041, and CLM-7049. CLM-7038 was valid despite initial rejection. Channel and amount are not decisive; independently verify incident, damage, repairs, coverage, claimant details, and payout.
- Home claims can be valid across paper, online, and phone channels. Phone storm claims CLM-7044–7046 were initially rejected but valid on appeal; do not reject solely for insufficient initial evidence when clarification or appeal is possible. Online CLM-7047–7048 were fraudulent, while online CLM-7036 was valid. Verify event, damage evidence, repair costs, coverage, and consistency.
- Health claims can be valid or fraudulent regardless of channel and size. Fraudulent examples include online CLM-7042–7043; CLM-7050 was a valid paper claim despite initial rejection. Valid large online claims include CLM-7034 and CLM-7039. Confirm coverage, treatment dates, provider records, and medical necessity; seek clarification rather than automatically rejecting incomplete documentation.
- Payout size is unreliable: small claims may be valid or fraudulent, and large claims may be valid. For every claim, avoid unsupported approval and premature rejection; use investigation, documentation requests, and appeal review where available.

Working notes:

- Do not treat any single channel, category, or payout size as determinative. Investigate before approval, but avoid unsupported or premature rejection; request documentation, clarification, and use appeal review where available.
- Auto paper is high risk but not uniformly fraudulent: prior paper cases were fraudulent, yet CLM-7059 was valid on appeal. - Home claims are mixed across channels. Fraudulent online claims include CLM-7047–7048, 7053, and 7058; valid examples include online CLM-7036 and paper CLM-7055 on appeal. - Health claims are mixed regardless of channel or amount. Fraudulent online claims include CLM-7042–7043 and 7060. Valid claims include paper CLM-7050, 7051, 7052, and 7059? [No: 7059 is auto], phone CLM-7056, and large online CLM-7034 and 7039. CLM-7051, 7052, and 7056 were valid on appeal despite initial rejection. Confirm coverage, treatment dates, provider records, and medical necessity; incomplete records warrant investigation or clarification, not automatic rejection.
- Payout size is unreliable: small and large claims can be either valid or fraudulent. Independent verification and consistent evidence are required for every claim.

Working notes:

- No single channel, category, or payout size is determinative. Investigate claim-specific evidence; do not automatically approve or reject. Request missing documentation, clarification, and use appeal review where available.
- Auto claims remain mixed across channels and amounts. Fraudulent examples include CLM-7022, 7024, 7026, 7035, 7037, 7040–7041, 7049, and 7054; valid examples include CLM-7038, 7057, 7059, 7065, 7068, and 7070. Check incident and liability details, damage photos, estimates/invoices, coverage, claimant information, and payout consistency.
- Home claims are also mixed. Fraudulent examples include online CLM-7047–7048, 7053, 7058, and paper CLM-7064 and 7069. Valid examples include online CLM-7036, paper CLM-7055, 7066, and phone CLM-7044–7046 and 7061. Verify event occurrence, damage evidence, repair costs, coverage, and consistency. Large paper claims require especially careful verification, but filing method alone is not grounds for rejection.
- Health claims vary regardless of channel or amount. Fraudulent examples include online CLM-7042–7043, 7060, and paper CLM-7062. Valid examples include paper CLM-7050–7052, phone CLM-7056, 7063, 7067, and large online CLM-7034 and 7039. Confirm coverage, treatment dates, provider records, and medical necessity; incomplete records justify investigation or clarification, not automatic rejection.
- Payout size is unreliable: small and large claims can be valid or fraudulent. Approve when documentation supports the loss and requested amount; reject only when evidence or audit establishes fraud or material inconsistency.
